details:
WHAT IT DOES

The Astronomican is a space mission design game. You design a complete mission, launch it, and learn why it worked (or didn't). Every choice has a consequence: a better instrument means more science, but also more mass, power, data and cost. Play it in the browser (no install): https://bakruu.github.io/The-Astronomican/

HOW IT WORKS

The game follows the phases of NASA's Mission Design Lab and JPL's Concept Maturity Levels: Office Hours, Concept, Trade Studies and Point Design.

1. Office Hours: pick an objective: Forest Watch (Earth observation, easy), Lunar Ice Hunter (medium), Buried Ice of Mars (hard) or Sandbox.

2. Trade Studies: choose the orbit, launch vehicle, spacecraft bus, power, battery, computer, attitude control, radio, ground stations and science instruments. A live dashboard shows mass, power, eclipse energy, data downlink and budget, and a design review explains every problem in plain language. A Flight Director box always tells new players what to fix next, and a 5-step tutorial explains the screen.

3. Go/No-Go poll: in team mode every role must say GO before launch, and any design change resets the poll.

4. Operations: the mission is simulated over its lifetime with random events such as solar storms, micrometeoroids, reaction-wheel failures and ground-station outages.

5. Mission report: a grade and score, lessons learned, a comparison with a real NASA mission (Landsat 9, Lunar Trailblazer, LRO, MRO/SHARAD, Hubble/JWST) and the attempt history, so players redesign and fly again.

SOLO OR TEAM

Up to 4 players can split the mission along NASA's four mission segments: Launch & Orbit (launch segment), Spacecraft (space segment), Ground & Comms (ground segment) and Science (user segment). This teaches that a mission only works when every segment agrees.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Systems engineering is usually taught with documents and spreadsheets. The Astronomican turns the same trade-offs into a 5-minute, mouse-only game that anyone can play on any computer. Players learn by failing safely: change one thing, fly again and see the effect. Part values are simplified but kept in realistic ranges based on NASA resources.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Unity 6 (URP) and C#, with the UI built from code; Blender for the 3D spacecraft part models; WebGL build hosted on GitHub Pages, plus a downloadable Mac build. Source code is open on GitHub.

USE OF AI

The code was developed with the help of Claude Code (Anthropic), an AI coding assistant. The game design, mission content and testing were done by our team.
